title: Energisers Without the Cringe (And With a Point)
author: Workshopbank
summary: Workshopbank argues that most workplace energisers fail because they generate energy for its own sake without producing anything the next activity can use, spending facilitator goodwill on activities participants correctly read as filler. The piece sets a two-job test for any energiser - reset the room's energy and feed the session that follows - and offers seven specific techniques (the Scale Walk, One-Word Check-In, Partner Swap, Wall Vote, 60-Second Silent Write, Headline Challenge, and Reverse Brainstorm) that each produce a concrete artifact, a rating, a written answer, a forced choice, that the facilitator uses immediately afterward. It directly engages a facilitator's counter-argument that these techniques prioritize individual reflection over group bonding, conceding the point but distinguishing sessions meant to build connection from sessions meant to produce work, arguing the latter is where most professional facilitation actually happens. The piece closes with a worked example showing the Scale Walk turning a sluggish post-lunch session into a substantive disagreement about the morning's decisions, arguing that is what real energy-reset looks like versus a Mexican wave.
points: Reframes the entire category of 'energiser' around a testable question - what does this produce for the next activity - rather than treating energy or fun as sufficient justification on its own.

Supplies seven distinct, immediately reusable techniques, each engineered to leave the facilitator with a concrete artifact (a spatial map of opinion, a written commitment, a forced binary choice) rather than just a temporarily livelier room.

Explicitly engages and partially concedes the strongest counter-argument - that true energisers should build group connection, not individual reflection - while defending the reflection-first approach for sessions oriented toward work rather than bonding.
Identifies goodwill and participant trust as a finite resource that low-value energisers visibly spend, reframing the choice of activity as a credibility decision, not just a pacing decision.

Demonstrates the framework's payoff with a concrete before/after scenario, showing how the Scale Walk converts a slumping post-lunch room into a substantive disagreement about the morning's actual decisions.
quotes: Your participants are professionals. They didn't give up a day of work to do star jumps. When an energiser is energy for its own sake, they feel it, and the goodwill you spend is hard to get back.
An energiser has two jobs: reset the energy in the room, and feed the session that's coming next. Do only the first and it's an extended break that wastes their time.
the walking wakes the body up before you ask the brain to work, and you're left with a visible map of where the room sits, which is your material for the next twenty minutes
Sitting and listening is receiving. The moment a pen goes down on paper, people switch to producing, and that switch is the reset.

Reverse each one, and the list of ways to fail turns into a list of the things the team has to get right. The pattern underneath all seven: each one connects to the topic. Each one also produces something you use next.

But most of the sessions I run aren't warming up for connection. They're warming up for work. And for that, energy on its own is a cost. I change the state of a group by putting the work in front of them, not by generating energy for its own sake.
Now two of them are arguing, warmly, about something that matters, and the slump is gone. Not from star jumps. From standing inside a disagreement about their own work and wanting to sort it out.
Your participants give you their time on trust. Spend 10 minutes of it on something that goes nowhere and that trust goes down.
